item.text: {"text":"Replacing a history item with PAD and recomputing the key-padding mask removes that position as an attention source. Restoring its clean residual activation alone cannot restore its influence on other tokens: its keys/values remain blocked in every subsequent layer. PAD queries may still produce nonzero outputs, but those outputs cannot transmit through masked keys/values. Replacing content with another non-PAD item preserves the attention pathway, making residual restoration informative. Keep sequence length, positions and padding mask fixed to isolate content effects; physically deleting tokens can also change positional embeddings. These conclusions follow from [PyTorch’s key-padding-mask semantics](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.modules.activation.MultiheadAttention.html); unmasking a PAD-corrupted position would be an additional intervention.\n\nFor a standard two-layer BERT4Rec with position-wise normalization/FFNs and final appended-MASK readout, the computational graph implies that useful history-token patches include input embeddings, residuals entering layer 1, layer-1 attention/FFN outputs, and the residual entering layer-2 attention. Each has a remaining attention operation that can carry restored information to MASK, provided the history position is unmasked. Layer-2 history keys/values can directly affect MASK; layer-2 history queries cannot affect another position’s output. History-token patches after layer-2 attention—including its attention output, FFN output or final residual—have no remaining cross-position route and therefore cannot change the MASK readout. Patching MASK itself remains effective downstream and provides a restoration control. This is an architectural inference from [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690), using the clean-to-corrupted intervention described in [activation patching](https://www.neelnanda.io/mechanistic-interpretability/attribution-patching)."}
